html:
The writing system of Ethiopia and Eritrea, which grew out of South Arabian writing in the first millennium BCE and is still used today for Amharic, Tigrinya and other languages.

The oldest inscriptions in the region, found in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia from around the 8th century BCE, use the alphabet of Saba in southern Arabia. Over time local scribes adapted it to write their own language, Ge'ez. At first it showed only consonants.

In the kingdom of Aksum, around the 4th century CE, scribes began to add small marks to each consonant to show the vowel that followed. This turned the script into an abugida, in which each character stands for a syllable. The change came around the time King Ezana made Aksum Christian, and the Bible was translated into Ge'ez soon after.

Ge'ez stopped being spoken many centuries ago but lives on as the language of worship in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Its script, with hundreds of syllable signs, is one of the few ancient African writing systems still in daily use.
sum: The writing system of Ethiopia and Eritrea, which grew out of South Arabian writing in the first millennium BCE and is still used today for Amharic, Tigrinya and other languages.
